https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Morocco’s foreign minister, Nasser Bourita, sits next to Donald Trump as he holds up the signed founding charter of his Board of Peace in January. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Morocco’s foreign minister, Nasser Bourita, sits next to Donald Trump as he holds up the signed founding charter of his Board of Peace in January. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty Images Morocco ‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disaster Washington-Rabat ties under scrutiny as questions swirl over what led to deadly influx into tiny Spanish territory Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Thu 6 Aug 2026 05.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he cosy relationship between Washington and Rabat has long been flaunted by both sides, from Morocco’s announcement this year that it would be the first African state to join Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to the congratulatory message recently sent by Trump to mark King Mohammed VI’s 27 years in power. The latest example landed this week. As Spain grappled with the aftermath of the sudden influx – and swift return – of more than 70,000 people into Ceuta, Morocco’s monarch confirmed he had named a $1bn highway flanking the disputed territory of Western Sahara after Trump. The deepening ties have come under renewed scrutiny as questions continue to swirl over what exactly led to the deadly mass border crossing into the tiny Spanish territory in north Africa . “I think there’s enough evidence to hypothesise or claim that Morocco is behind this,” said Riccardo Fabiani, the north Africa project director for the International Crisis Group. “But there was no clear trigger for this, and this is what is puzzling for everyone.” 0:44 Migrants in Spain’s Ceuta enclave escorted back to Morocco – video Observers have suggested Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s archrival, Algeria, could have set off Morocco. But another, perhaps more plausible explanation pointed towards the US, said Fabiani. “It’s obviously impossible to demonstrate,” he said. “But in terms of plausibility, I don’t think it’s impossible to imagine that Morocco might have done something to earn brownie points with its allies, given that Morocco and this particular administration in Washington do have a very close, excellent relationship.” While Morocco had probably not “masterminded” the surge into Ceuta, he said, its relationship with the Trump administration – along with the Moroccan king’s desire to keep its claim to Ceuta in the spotlight – may have affected how it responded to fast-spreading online rumours about the Spanish border being thrown open. View image in fullscreen A young person is escorted by Spanish security forces after attempting to cross into Ceuta on Saturday. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters “For sure the Moroccan security forces were monitoring those conversations,” said Fabiani. “They saw that and there was probably some conversation where they decided to do nothing and see where this goes.” What followed made headlines across the globe as tens of thousands of people swam or waded across one of the EU’s two land borders with Africa. As Spain scrambled to cope, far-right voices seized on the images. In the US, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the state department blamed the influx on the Socialist-led government of Spain, while Trump warned that electing Democrats would make what happened in Spain “look small-time”. At no point did any of them mention Morocco or the potential role it might have played. Trump and his administration have long been open about the deep antipathy they feel for Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, whose refusal to allow the US to use its airbases during the Iran war, rejection of the 5% defence spending target and vociferous criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza have arguably made Spain the administration’s least favourite EU country. The American response seemed to be a triumph for Rabat, whose relationship with the US president traces back to his first term, when Morocco agreed to normalise ties with Israel in exchange for Trump’s recognition of its sovereignty claim over the disputed territory of Western Sahara . Since then, Morocco’s all-powerful monarch had doubled down on outreach efforts, said Fabiani. “The Moroccans have really made extra efforts to cultivate every single major decision-maker within the administration, including the president himself, to make sure that this administration will support, until the end, the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara.” A hint that the relationship could help Morocco lay claim to more than Western Sahara came in a recent US congressional report that appeared to be sympathetic to Morocco’s refusal to recognise Ceuta as Spanish territory, describing it as “Spanish-administered” rather than a part of Spain, as it has been since 1580. Days after the influx, interest in Ceuta remained heightened among those close to both Trump and the Israeli government, said Haizam Amirah-Fernández, the director of the Madrid-based Centre for Contemporary Arab Studies. “They haven’t stopped talking about Ceuta for several days in a row, which is quite striking.” View image in fullscreen Red Cross personnel distributing food at Trampolín beach in Ceuta this week. Photograph: REDUAN/EPA What had been laid bare was Rabat’s willingness to use “hybrid tactics to achieve political objectives”, said Amirah-Fernández, drawing a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls to allow more than 8,000 people to cross into Ceuta in a show of anger over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara pro-independence leader to travel to Spain to be treated for Covid-19. This time around, as nearly 10 times more people crossed into Ceuta, it set off a bout of finger-pointing across the EU rather than any kind of concerted effort to push back using the bloc’s status as Morocco’s largest trading partner and largest foreign investor. “The reaction of several governments in the EU was, in the end, what the White House was looking for – the erosion of solidarity between European partners,” said Amirah-Fernández. Senior officials in Morocco have pushed back against accusations it was in any way complicit. View image in fullscreen King Mohammed VI and Trump in 2018. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images At the Rabat-based Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, there was little doubt that relations between Morocco and the US were in their “golden era”. Even so, the country’s approach to the Trump administration remained pragmatic, said Said Saddiki, a senior fellow at the institute. “Moroccan policymakers are well aware of President Trump’s transactional style and have sought to preserve Morocco’s strategic autonomy,” Saddiki said in an email, citing efforts to maintain partnerships with the EU, China and the Gulf states, among others. “The relationship with the Trump administration has strengthened Morocco’s international position, but so far it has not come at the expense of its relations with Spain or the European Union.” For Fabiani, the events in Ceuta served to underscore the perils of Europe’s reliance on north African states to control migration flows. “This has made Europe entirely vulnerable and dependent on the goodwill of a country like Morocco,” he said. “Morocco is a partner, but at the same time it has its own interests. This vulnerability was on show.” This weakness could become more of an issue as time passed, given Morocco’s perception that the issue of Ceuta remained unsettled, Fabiani warned. “And Morocco feels emboldened, and there is an administration in Washington that is willing to back it up,” he said. “I don’t think Europe is ready for what comes next because it could get much more complicated.” Explore more on these topics Morocco Donald Trump US foreign policy Spain Migration Refugees Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/02/eu-.text: Menü Kereső Oroszország eszkalált, együtt kell élnie a következményekkel – figyelmeztetett a német külügyminiszter Gazdaság frissítve Márton Balázs Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Fontos, hogy Oroszország világosan lássa: Európa összetart – közölte az uniós külügyminiszterek szerdai ülésére érkezve Johann Wadephul. A német külügyminiszter azután beszélt erről az írországi Druids Glenben, hogy a német hatóságok szerint Oroszország megbízásából kísérelhettek meg egy meghiúsult támadást a lipcsei repülőtéren egy robbanószerrel felszerelt drónnal. Wadephul közölte: Oroszország eszkalált, együtt kell élnie a következményekkel. A következő hetekben célzottan kell dolgozni azon, hogy újabb személyeket vegyenek fel a szankciós listára, ami „sokakat” érint majd. Felszólított Ukrajna támogatásának fokozására a tél előtt, különösen a légvédelemnél. Wadephul X-en is egyesével megköszönte a kollégái üzeneteit, köztük Orbán Anita kiállását és „világos szavait”. A magyar tárcavezető arról írt: mélységesen aggasztó, hogy az orosz hibrid tevékenység számban és intenzitásban is nő Európában. A „közelmúltbeli német incidensek egyre veszélyesebb és vakmerőbb viselkedésmintát mutatnak”, ami komolyan veszélyezteti Európa biztonságát. Magyarország teljesen szolidáris Németországgal, és kész támogatni a partnereit a hibrid fenyegetések elhárításában. Világos, hogy a lipcsei támadás az államilag szponzorált terrorizmus jegyeit viseli magán – jelentette ki Kaja Kallas. Az Európai Unió külügyi és biztonságpolitikai főképviselője arról beszélt, több tagállamban behívták az orosz nagyköveteket, megvitatják, mit tehetnek. Emlékeztetett rá, hogy korábbról már folyamatban van több mint 1600 személy, cég felvétele a szankciós listára, de erről nem ma döntenek, mert a mai egy informális találkozó. Helen McEntee ír külügyminiszter az uniós miniszteri Tanács soros elnökségének nevében teljes szolidaritásáról biztosította nem csak a német, hanem az észt kollégáját is, mivel ott és más uniós tagállamokban – például Lengyelországban, Lettországban, Romániában – is hasonló eseteket láttak az utóbbi hónapokban. Már nem csak hibrid fenyegetésekről, hanem „jelentős tevékenységről” van szó. Világosnak látta, hogy Oroszország megpróbálja megosztani őket és megfélemlíteni a lakosaikat. Többet kell tenniük és fenntartaniuk a nyomást Oroszországon. Oroszország megpróbál megosztani és elrettenteni minket, az Egyesült Királyság nevében világosan kijelenthetem: ez kudarcot fog vallani – közölte Ed Miliband, akit több más EU-n kívüli ország külügyminiszterével együtt hívtak meg. Több hibrid beavatkozást és drónbehatolást tapasztaltak az utóbbi időben – figyelmeztetett Oana-Silvia Țoiu román külügyminiszter. Beszélt a német kollégájával, szolidárisak a hibrid fenyegetésekkel szemben, és ennek megfelelően fognak diplomáciai téren is fellépni. Oroszország erősíti a hibrid hadjáratát, mondta a lipcsei támadáskísérletről Elina Valtonen finn külügyminiszter, aki szerint fokozni kell rajta a nyomást. Világos, hogy ez lesz az egyes számú téma, jelentette ki Josef Schellhorn osztrák külügyminiszter, szolidárisak Németországgal. Petr Macinka cseh külügyminiszter az MTI szerint nyugtalanítónak nevezte a német hatóságok megállapítását, hogy a lipcsei repülőtéren történt drónincidens mögött Oroszország áll. Írországból visszatérve Prágában meg akarja vitatni az ügyet a cseh hírszerzéssel is, amelynek szerinte biztos vannak saját értesülései is. Kérdésre válaszolva megerősítette: hivatalába kérette Anna Ponomarjovát, Oroszország prágai nagykövetét, hogy adjon magyarázatot a történtekre. Megint pedzegetik az EU-ban befagyasztott orosz vagyon felhasználását Már nem hibridek, hanem nagyon is kinetikusak az orosz támadások Kęstutis Budris litván külügyminiszter szerint . Oroszországnak ez egy olcsó módszer, hogy növelje a társadalmi feszültségeket, ezért a céljuk, hogy megmutassák: „ez nem fog megfélemlíteni minket” és elrettenteni Ukrajna támogatásától, a nyomás fenntartásától Oroszországon. Úgy vélte, a Kreml azt akarja bemutatni az orosz törvényhozási választás előtt, hogy azt tehet Európában, amit akar. A mostani jó alkalom lenne, hogy beszéljenek a befagyasztott orosz vagyonról – utalt az EU-ban ragadt orosz jegybanki vagyonra, amelynek a felhasználásával tavaly egy hitelt terveztek Ukrajnának (ezt többek között az Orbán-kormány ellenezte). Az orosz vagyont ugyan az Ukrajna elleni háború végéig és orosz jóvátételig befagyasztották , de végül a közös uniós költségvetés fedezetével adtak – három országra, köztük Magyarországra pénzügyi terhet nem rovó – kölcsönt. Akkor az állam- és kormányfők testületét vezető António Costa kijelentette : az EU fenntartja a jogot, hogy a befagyasztott orosz vagyont használják, és folytatják a munkát ezen, ez a 27-ből 25 vezető nevében kiadott következtetésekben is megjelent. Néhány napja egy holland–lengyel–spanyol–svéd levél újra pedzegetni kezdte , hogy foglalkozzanak a kérdéssel. A külügyminiszterek hagyományosan augusztus végén – szeptember elején ülnek össze egy informális találkozóra a Tanács soros elnökének országában, ettől az utóbbi években csak a 2024-es magyar elnökség alatt tértek el . Az informális üléseken nem hoznak döntéseket, így konkrét lépések a mostanin sem várhatóak. A NATO-főtitkárral egyeztetett az Európai Bizottság elnöke Azért találkozunk, hogy beszéljünk Oroszország lipcsei támadásáról – közölte szerdán Ursula von der Leyen. Az Európai Bizottság elnöke Mark Ruttét, az Észak-atlanti Szerződés Szervezetének (NATO-nak) a főtitkárát fogadta az uniós testület brüsszeli központjában. Von der Leyen leszögezte: ha a támadás sikeres lett volna, óriási károkat okozott volna és akár életekbe is kerülhetett volna, „úgyhogy nagyon világos szeretnék lenni abban, hogy ez mi volt. Ez egy katonai minőségű anyagokat felhasználó támadás volt, amelyet orosz ügynökök hajtottak végre az EU területén, és ezt nem fogjuk eltűrni.” A megfélemlítés „nem fog működni”, egységesek, és a NATO-val együtt növelni fogják a nyomást Oroszországon. Lipcse eszkaláció, de egy nagyobb mintázatba illeszkedik egyre veszélyesebb incidensekkel. Több szankciót tartott szükségesnek, és kiemelte, hogy meg kell védeni a mindennapi infrastruktúrát. Oroszország egyre vakmerőbb, az egész NATO szolidáris Németországgal, az egységünk megingathatatlan – hangsúlyozta Rutte. Cikkünket kiegészítettük Von der Leyen és Rutte egyeztetésével. https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text: By Mark Kersten Published On 15 Sep 2026 15 Sep 2026 Save Share Canada, the UK and Australia should investigate the WCK attack in Gaza on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google People gather around the carcass of a car used by US-based aid group World Central Kitchen, that was attacked by the Israeli army in Deir al-Balah in the central Gaza Strip on April 2, 2024 [AFP] The Israeli army has concluded its probe into the 2024 drone strikes that killed seven humanitarian workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK). The verdict? No criminal investigation is warranted. No explanation was provided. The decision not to pursue criminal responsibility for the attack was slammed by Western states as “shameful”. Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand called it “unacceptable”. The Australian government said it was “outraged”. The Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared it was “ disappointed ”. If Western states are indeed dissatisfied with the outcome of the Israeli probe, then they should investigate the crime themselves. They have the institutional capacity and legal right to do so. Not pursuing an investigation would mean they accept Israeli impunity for the killing of their aid workers in Gaza. Images taken in the wake of the drone strikes on the WCK convoy show a charred hole where Israeli missiles breached the roof of the organisation’s vehicles – right next to its logo. The three cars in the WCK convoy were clearly marked, and their movements across the Gaza Strip were coordinated in real time with Israeli forces. Such precautions were not enough to protect the lives of Lalzawmi Frankcom (Australia, 43 years old), Damian Sobol (Poland, 35), Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha (Palestine, 25), Jacob Flickinger (dual citizen of the US and Canada, 33), or British citizens John Chapman (57), James Henderson (33) and James Kirby (47). They are among the more than 1,000 humanitarian aid workers killed in Gaza since 2023. Advertisement The attack on the WCK convoy has the hallmarks of a potential war crime. Canada’s Anand intimated as much when she referred to the laws of armed conflict in stating that “Canada expects international humanitarian law to be upheld”. Importantly, even if the attack was conducted in error, as Israel has claimed, it may still constitute a war crime. Calling an attack a “tragic mistake” is not a magic wand that absolves perpetrators of responsibility. If those involved in the strikes were acting recklessly, with clear disregard for civilian life, they may be liable for war crimes under international law. The commander who ordered the strikes on the WCK convoy, Colonel Nochi Mendel, said in an interview, “I am not sorry for what I did.” That an Israeli officer is showing no remorse for taking civilian life is hardly surprising. A culture of impunity breeds under such conditions, one in which perpetrators do not fear the consequences of their actions. Indeed, it is almost certain that the Israeli army has calculated that, however angry Western powers are over the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation, it is just hot air and will not be met with action. Those powers should prove them wrong. London, Canberra and Ottawa have stated they will “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the families of those slain in the WCK attack. But they should not waste their time seeking them from those who have clearly demonstrated no interest in holding those responsible for the WCK attack accountable. They should instead act themselves. The United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have the legal authority, expertise and resources to exercise jurisdiction over atrocity crimes committed in Gaza. They can do so by exercising what is called universal jurisdiction, which allows states to investigate and prosecute international crimes – war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide – even when committed abroad by foreigners against foreigners. In this instance, those killed include their own citizens. Their obligations and interest to pursue accountability are thus even more obvious. So, what should happen next? Canada, the UK and Australia should announce a joint criminal investigation into suspected war crimes committed in the WCK attack. They can also invite other states to join in. Poland, for example, also has the legal ability to exercise universal jurisdiction. Canada has already taken some steps in investigating war crimes in Palestine. In 2024, the Canadian police launched a “structural investigation” into international crimes committed in Gaza. This process collects evidence that can be used later in cases against perpetrators who enter Canadian jurisdiction. Advertisement Of course, just opening a criminal investigation does not mean that anyone will be prosecuted. But it could provide the victims’ families their best shot at seeking justice. It would be a sign that states are willing to dedicate resources to holding perpetrators accountable. Moreover, if warrants are ultimately issued by Canada, the UK and Australia, and if any of the suspected perpetrators travel abroad, they could potentially be subject to extradition to one of the countries to be prosecuted. The decision to dismiss a criminal investigation into the WCK attacks is indeed unacceptable. And those states whose citizens were killed must pursue their own criminal inquiry into the suspected war crimes committed against humanitarians in Gaza. The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://mymotherlode.com/news/national/1.text: 58.5 ° F Full Weather | Burn Info Sponsored By: Belarus frees 25 prisoners in exchange for the US lifting some sanctions, envoy says Sponsored by: Add us as a preferred source By AP News Published Sep 16, 2026 5:22 am Updated Sep 16, 2026 8:55 am Belarus Lukashenko View Photos TALLINN, Estonia (AP) — The U.S. special envoy for Belarus said Wednesday that the country’s authorities have agreed to release 25 prisoners in exchange for the lifting of U.S. sanctions against two Belarusian companies. John Coale, President Donald Trump’s special envoy for Belarus, made the statement a day after meeting Belarus’ authoritarian President Alexander Lukashenko, who pushed for the remaining U.S. sanctions against his country to be lifted. “25 prisoners are free today!” Coale said on X, adding that “President Trump’s commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results.” He also thanked Lukashenko and authorities in Lithuania, a European Union member that neighbors Belarus, for their support. “We will continue to improve U.S.-Belarus relations and are working to secure the release of more people in the very near future,” Coale said. “We are not finished!” Speaking to reporters in Minsk, Coale said as part of what he called “an interim deal” and “as a show of good will,” Belarus will release 25 people in exchange for the U.S. lifting sanctions on two Belarusian companies, Lakokraska and Bellesbumprom. He added that further release of prisoners and the lifting of more sanctions will follow later after all details are agreed upon. Belarusian authorities haven’t announced any details of the prisoners’ release yet. Lukashenko has governed the nation of 9.5 million with an iron fist for more than three decades, and the country has been sanctioned repeatedly by Western countries — both for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing Moscow to use its territory to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since Trump returned to the White House for his second term, Lukashenko has released hundreds of political prisoners in a series of U.S.-mediated deals that also lifted some U.S. sanctions. Belarusian opposition leader-in-exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya welcomed the prisoners’ release, but noted that many others remain in custody. “This is an important step, but only a step,” Tsikhanouskaya told The Associated Press. “Many political prisoners remain behind bars.” For Lukashenko, “people are bargaining chips — something he can trade and then replace with new hostages,” she said, adding that “we have to break this vicious cycle of repression.” Belarus still has 887 political prisoners, according to the Viasna human rights center. Tsikhanouskaya, who met the freed prisoners in the Lithuanian capital of Vilnius, said the prisoners’ release shouldn’t be seen as a sign of political change in Belarus. “Repressions are continuing,” she said. “Ultimately, every political prisoner must be released.” As part of a deal in March that Washington helped broker, Lukashenko ordered the release of 250 political prisoners, while the U.S. agreed to lift sanctions on two Belarusian state banks and the country’s Finance Ministry, and to remove the top Belarusian potash producers from a sanctions list. Another deal in April released prominent journalist Andrzej Poczobut in a swap with Poland that saw a total of 10 people freed. Lukashenko’s rule was challenged after a 2020 presidential election, when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to protest a vote they viewed as rigged. In an ensuing crackdown, tens of thousands were detained, with many beaten by police. Prominent opposition figures fled the country or were imprisoned. Five years after the mass demonstrations, Lukashenko won a seventh term last year in an election that the opposition called a farce. Among the prisoners released Wednesday were media managers Andrei Aliaksandrau and Liudmila Chekina and journalists Dzmitry Navazhylau and Kiryl Pazniak. Pavel Sapelka, a lawyer with the Viasna human rights center, said that Belarusian authorities confiscated passports of some of those released in what he said amounted to “forced deportation.” “Lukashenko’s regime is simply throwing dissidents out, getting rid of dangerous voices inside the country,” Sapelka told the AP. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxdd.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pneumonic plague is often described as the most virulent form of plague By Dominic Hughes Health correspondent Published 6 October 2026 The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information on the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory. It is still not clear exactly what led to the worker falling ill, but media reports have led to a flurry of speculation. Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague. So what is pneumonic plague, and how dangerous is it? What is pneumonic plague? Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood. Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types. Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood. It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague. The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases. Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States. Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford. He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis , persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world. "Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa. "Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact." How does it spread? Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas. You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal. But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact. You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs. Some theories suggest that pneumonic plague was one of the main drivers behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century. Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague. "I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said. "Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form. "Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism. "This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks." Can it be treated? According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours. If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal. But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early. Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health. "Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease. "Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age. "It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early. "That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine." In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague. The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" â and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened. US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States". The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".
